title: Estimating a job from labour, materials and extras
audience: Owners of small Australian service businesses who prepare estimates for jobs that are more than a quick fix
learningOutcomes: Build an estimate that shows labour, materials, subcontract costs, permits, cleanup and travel as separate lines.
Estimate job time from a checked scope and the owner's own record of similar jobs.
Identify the assumptions and risks that could change the estimate, and state them in the quote.

instruction.heading: Check the site before pricing
instruction.body: An estimate built from a photo or a phone description often misses access problems, the condition of surfaces and hidden work. Visit the site when the job is not simple. Note the access route, the working height where relevant, the condition of surfaces or items, any existing conditions that affect the work and any hazards that need controls. Write down what was seen in the same terms that will appear in the scope. Where a site is unsafe, or the work lies outside the owner's permitted scope, record that and refer the work before pricing it.

instruction.heading: Writing the scope and estimating the time
instruction.body: Write the scope as an ordered list of tasks, with the finish expected for each. Estimate the time for each task from the owner's records of similar past jobs. Where no record exists, time a sample task, note the result and update the estimate after the job. A trade article from Carters Trade Leader suggests comparing the original quote with the actual labour time, then feeding the gap into the next quote. Add time for setup, travel, cleanup and handover. A scope that says clean the rooms is weak. A scope that names the rooms, the tasks in each, the materials or products and the finish expected is useful.

instruction.heading: Pricing labour, materials and extras
instruction.body: Labour is the time for each task multiplied by the hourly rate from “Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”, or the minimum charge if that is higher. Materials are the cost of each item, including delivery and an allowance for waste where the task needs one. A subcontract line is the quoted price of a licensed or specialist provider brought in, and the owner must check that the subcontractor holds the required licence and insurance before the line is added. Cleanup and waste disposal are costs too, and so are fuel and travel if they are not already in labour. Show each cost on its own line, so the client can see where the money goes.

instruction.heading: Stating what could change the price
instruction.body: List the assumptions behind the estimate, such as the access, the condition of the surfaces or items, the existing conditions and the client's choice of finish. Add a clear line that names what would trigger a variation, and state that the variation will be agreed in writing before the extra work starts. An estimate that names its risks protects both the owner and the client when the job reveals more than was expected. Some estimating guides add 10 to 20 percent to estimates for unexpected work; if the owner does so, state the allowance as an assumption.

procedure: Visit the site for any job that is not simple, and record access, working height where relevant, condition, existing conditions that affect the work and hazards.
Write the scope as an ordered list of tasks, with the expected finish for each task.
Estimate the time for each task from the owner's records, and add setup, travel, cleanup and handover time.
Price labour from the billable time and the rate, and price materials with delivery and waste.
Add subcontract, permit, inspection, cleanup and travel lines where they apply.
List the assumptions and variation triggers, and check the subtotal before any markup is applied (“Markup, margin and presenting the final quote”).

workedExamples.situation: A job has a main task the owner can perform, a separate specialist task outside the owner's own skills, materials to supply and waste to remove.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which lines should the estimate show, and which work should be referred?
workedExamples.reasoning: The estimate should show the owner's labour, the materials, the waste removal and travel as separate lines. The specialist task becomes a subcontract line only if the specialist holds the licence for that work in the state or territory and the required insurance; otherwise it is referred to a licensed provider.

equipmentAndPpe: Site visit checklist covering access, working height where relevant, condition, existing conditions and hazards
Estimate template with separate cost lines

commonErrors.error: Estimating from a photo alone, then finding extra work on site.
commonErrors.prevention: Visit the site for any job that is not simple, and list the assumptions in the estimate.

commonErrors.error: Leaving cleanup, travel, disposal and permits out of the estimate.
commonErrors.prevention: Show each as a separate line, even when the amount is small.

commonErrors.error: Using a subcontractor who is not licensed or insured for the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence, the scope and the insurance certificate before adding the subcontract line.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Permits, approvals and inspections, where they apply, depend on the type of work and the local council or other authority. Check the rules for the council and the state or territory before pricing.

A subcontractor doing licensed work must hold the licence for that work. Whether an unlicensed subcontractor may do licensed work is set by state or territory rules, so check them before engaging anyone. This lesson does not grant any licence.

qualityStandard: Each estimate line is shown separately, and every cost is traced to a supplier price, a rate or a recorded time.
The scope lists the tasks in order, with the expected finish for each.
Assumptions and variation triggers are stated in the estimate.
documentationEvidence: Site visit notes, with photos taken with the client's consent
Estimate showing labour, materials, subcontract, permit, cleanup and travel lines
Assumptions and variation list, sent with the quote
summary: Visit the site for any job that is not simple, and write the scope in order.
Show each cost as a separate line, including cleanup and travel.
State the assumptions and variation triggers before adding the markup.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why should a non-simple job be visited before it is priced?
options: Because a visit is billed at double the rate for the trip
Because access, condition and hidden work often change the price
Because the client's paint colour has to be chosen on site
Because a photo cannot be shared with the client

knowledgeChecks.question: Which item should be a separate estimate line rather than part of labour or materials?
A subcontractor has been quoted for a licensed task. What must the owner check?
options: Only that the price is low and that the quote was sent quickly by email
That the subcontractor holds the required licence and insurance for the work
That the subcontractor has a social media page with many followers and good photos
Nothing, because the owner is responsible only for their own work
